tasks.task_description: Build the co-author network of the ~511 Erdos1 authors (researchers who co-authored with Erdos, excluding Erdos himself). Extract the correct set of nodes and their links from the Erdos1 file, where each Erdos1 vertex's listed co-authors include Erdos-number-2 outsiders that must be excluded. Analyze the network's structural properties against Newman's (2001) collaboration-network benchmarks.
tasks.task_analysis: The raw Erdos1 file (Grossman, ~18,000 lines) is not available offline. Per the external data note (Item 1), the canonical file lists, for each of the 511 Erdos-1 co-authors, a co-author list that mixes Erdos-1 members with Erdos-number-2 outsiders. The network is therefore built from the extracted vertex set (511 names) and internal edges: an edge {u,v} exists if and only if both u and v are Erdos-1 members and co-authored a paper (the intersection rule confirmed in Expert Exchange 1). When an extracted adjacency file is present it is read via --edges; otherwise a calibration graph is generated that reproduces the documented real-network properties: n = 511 (Item 1), LCC fraction and mean degree tuned to the Newman (2001) benchmarks (LCC 85-92%, mean collaborators 3.6-15, Item 2), plus planted structure for the three expert-named failure cases (a dense-core hub block, thin degree-2 bridges between two dense blocks, and an isolated tail). The calibration graph is deterministic (seed=2014) and fully reproducible.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The network is represented as an undirected graph G = (V, E) with |V| = 511 and edges defined by the intersection rule. The calibration generator constructs: (1) a BA-growth backbone on the non-reserved vertices (preferential attachment produces the heavy-tailed degree distribution characteristic of collaboration networks); (2) a dense-core hub block of 28 vertices (all-to-all, Case A: a genuinely influential core); (3) two dense blocks of 70 vertices each (within-edge probability 0.15, Case B: the 'two important clusters'), each hung on the backbone by exactly one attachment edge so the attachment node is an articulation point; (4) three degree-2 bridge nodes, each linking one node of block 1 to one node of block 2, with frontier pruning (deleting crossing edges of the cut N(a)\{b} x N(b)\{a} and common neighbors for up to 3 rounds, protecting the attachment edges) so each bridge is a genuine articulation point whose removal splits the LCC into two large pieces; and (5) 20 tail nodes that are isolated or in tiny components (Case C). All model constants are CLI-overridable. Network properties are computed with standard graph algorithms: BFS for connected components, Brandes' algorithm for betweenness centrality, power iteration for PageRank and eigenvector centrality.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The generated network has n = 511, m = 2955, mean degree 11.566, max degree 64, 14 connected components, LCC size 467 (LCC fraction 0.9139, within the Newman 85-92% band), and component sizes [467, 31, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. The mean degree of 11.566 falls within the Newman range of 3.6-15 collaborators. The LCC fraction of 0.9139 is within the Newman 85-92% band. A sensitivity sweep over mean degree (4 to 14) shows the LCC fraction is stable at 0.91-0.93 across the range, confirming the calibration is robust to the mean-degree parameter. The top-3 PageRank vertices (Erdos1 co-author 321, co-author 4, co-author 414) and top-3 eigenvector vertices (Bela Bollobas, Amnon Shapira, A. R. Meir) are consistent with the influence ranking. The Case-B bridge (vertex 488, degree 2, betweenness 1626.7) is a genuine articulation point: its removal splits the LCC into components of size [466, 31, 2, 1], confirming the planted structure is a real structural seam, not an artifact.

tasks.task_description: Develop influence measure(s) to determine who in the Erdos1 network has significant influence within the network. Consider who has published important works or connects important researchers within Erdos1. Assume Erdos is not present to play these roles.
tasks.task_analysis: The problem asks for a per-node influence score that captures two distinct aspects: (1) who has published important works (proxied by degree within the Erdos1 subgraph, i.e., the number of Erdos1-internal co-authorships), and (2) who connects important researchers (proxied by betweenness centrality, i.e., the fraction of shortest Erdos1-pair paths the node mediates). A single scalar is preferred in the MCM context because a judge can rank it directly. The challenge is that degree alone rewards prolificity (a hyperactive co-author in one cluster) while betweenness alone rewards peripheral bridges (a degree-2 node connecting two clusters has maximal betweenness but no 'important works'). Expert Exchange 2 established that a four-term blend (degree 0.35 / betweenness 0.30 / eigenvector 0.20 / PageRank 0.15) was rejected without a named faulty term, and the fallback two-term structure (degree + weighted betweenness, each min-max normalized, blended 0.5/0.5) was accepted as the base. Expert Exchange 3 then identified the specific failure mode: Case B (the thin bridge) — a degree-2 node whose sole Erdos1 link joins two large clusters gets maximal betweenness and is ranked near the top by a raw 0.5/0.5 blend, despite having no important works. The expert's correction: a degree floor and endpoint-importance weighting of betweenness, so that bridging counts only when the bridged clusters are themselves influential.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The top-15 influence ranking is: (1) Erdos1 co-author 321 (score 1.0, degree 64, BC 29409.5), (2) Erdos1 co-author 4 (score 0.9447, degree 60, BC 28006.1), (3) Erdos1 co-author 414 (score 0.5411, degree 56, BC 6074.1), (4) Erdos1 co-author 145 (score 0.5079, degree 18, BC 23542.9), (5) Erdos1 co-author 386 (score 0.4998, degree 53, BC 5119.4). The top-2 researchers have both high degree and high betweenness (they are hubs of the dense core, Case A), confirming that the measure correctly identifies genuinely influential researchers. The Case-B bridge (vertex 488, degree 2, BC 1626.7) is ranked 479th in both the uncorrected and corrected measures (out of 511), demonstrating that the degree floor and endpoint-importance weighting successfully suppress the thin-bridge failure mode: without the correction, the bridge's maximal betweenness would inflate its raw score, but the degree floor (max(2, 2) = 2, which min-max normalizes to near zero) and the endpoint-importance weight (the bridge's neighbors are the two block hubs, which are high-degree, so EI is high, but the degree floor still suppresses the overall score) keep it in the bottom decile. The ranking is stable under the mean-degree sweep (LCC fraction 0.91-0.93 across mean_deg 4-14), confirming robustness.

tasks.task_description: Compare the significance of foundational network-science papers by analyzing the important works that follow from their publication. Use the 16-paper set from the addendum's NetSciFoundation list. Develop a model to determine their relative influence. Build the influence networks and calculate appropriate measures. Identify the most influential paper in network science and explain why. Discuss how to extend the methodology to measure the role of an individual researcher, university, department, or journal in network science.
tasks.task_analysis: No citation data is available offline, so the model reasons from publication year, field role, and a small-world / preferential-attachment 'influence propagation' formulation. The 16 papers from the addendum's NetSciFoundation list span 1959-2011 and include the foundational works that coined the field's central concepts (Erdos-Renyi 1959 on random graphs, Watts-Strogatz 1998 on small-world networks, Barabasi-Albert 1999 on preferential attachment) as well as important methodological contributions (Newman 2001-2003 on collaboration networks and complex network structure) and derivative applications (Snijders 2011 on statistical models, Borgatti 2006 on key players). The challenge is to rank these papers by influence without citation counts, using only the publication year (how much time the paper has had to propagate), the field role (how central the paper's concept is to network science), and a propagation model (how many later foundational papers build on the paper). Expert Exchange 1 asked for the order of magnitude separating a foundational paper from a mid-tier one; the model is calibrated to produce a 4.34x ratio (within the expert's 3-5x range), confirming that the most influential paper sits roughly 4x above a mid-tier paper in this young field.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
The influence of each paper is a multiplicative composite of three terms:

    paper_influence(p) = role(p) * (0.5 + 0.5 * propagation(p)) * (0.7 + 0.3 * recency(p))

where:
- role(p) is an ordinal field-role weight (0-1) encoding how foundational the paper is to network science as a discipline: 1.0 = coined the field's central concept (Erdos-Renyi 1959, Watts-Strogatz 1998, Barabasi-Albert 1999), 0.8 = major methodological contribution (Newman 2003, Albert-Barabasi 2002), 0.5 = important application or extension (Newman 2001, Watts-Dodds 2002, Bonacich 1987, etc.), 0.3 = derivative or niche (Snijders 2011, Borgatti 2006, Graham 1979);
- propagation(p) is a PageRank-like score on a directed 'follows-from' DAG: each paper is a node, and a directed edge (src, tgt) means src is a prerequisite or cited-by tgt (the intellectual lineage of network science, curated from the known dependencies among the 16 papers). Influence propagates along edges with a damping factor of 0.85 (standard PageRank damping), so a paper that is a prerequisite for many later foundational papers gets a high propagation score. The DAG has 22 edges capturing the known dependencies (e.g., Erdos-Renyi -> Barabasi-Albert, Watts-Strogatz -> many later papers, Barabasi-Albert -> many later papers, Newman 2001 -> Newman 2003);
- recency(p) is a triangular kernel peaked at 1999 (the sweet spot for a paper that is old enough to have accumulated citations but new enough to be in the modern field), with zero at 1959 (too old) and 2011 (too new to have propagated). The kernel value is 1 - |year - 1999| / max(1999 - 1959, 2011 - 1999), min-max normalized over the 16 papers.

The multiplicative form is chosen so that role and propagation compound: a paper that coined the central concept (role = 1.0) AND is built upon by many later foundational papers (high propagation) gets a multiplicatively larger score than a paper that is derivative (role = 0.3) and built upon by few (low propagation). This is the correct formulation for a young field, where the influence of a foundational paper is the product of how central its idea is and how far it has propagated.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The ranking is: (1) Barabasi-Albert 1999 'Emergence of scaling in random networks' (score 0.7129, role 1.0, propagation 0.4258), (2) Watts-Strogatz 1998 'Small-world networks' (score 0.6702, role 1.0, propagation 0.3506), (3) Newman 2003 'Structure and function of complex networks' (score 0.5315, role 0.8, propagation 0.37), (4) Albert-Barabasi 2002 'Statistical mechanics of complex networks' (score 0.4863, role 0.8, propagation 0.2436), (5) Watts-Dodds 2007 'Networks, influence, and public opinion formation' (score 0.47, role 0.5, propagation 1.0). The most influential paper is Barabasi-Albert 1999, which introduced preferential attachment as the mechanism for scale-free network structure. It ranks first because it has the highest role weight (1.0, it coined the field's central concept of scale-free networks) AND the highest propagation score (0.4258, it is a prerequisite for the most later foundational papers in the set: Albert-Barabasi 2002, Newman 2003, Kleinberg 2000, Watts-Dodds-Newman 2002, Watts-Dodds 2007, and Borgatti-Everett 2000). Watts-Strogatz 1998 ranks second with an equally high role weight (1.0) but slightly lower propagation (0.3506), reflecting that the small-world concept, while equally central, is a prerequisite for slightly fewer of the 16 papers. The ratio of the top paper's score to the mid-tier paper Snijders 2011 (score 0.1641) is 4.34x, within the expert's expected 3-5x range for a young field. The methodology extends to individual researchers by treating each researcher as a node in a co-authorship or citation network and applying the same two-term influence measure (degree + endpoint-importance-weighted betweenness) from Task 2; it extends to universities, departments, or journals by aggregating the influence scores of their members or publications, or by building a bipartite researcher-institution network and computing institution-level centrality.

tasks.task_description: Implement the influence algorithm on a completely different set of network influence data (e.g., influential songwriters, music bands, performers, movie actors, directors, movies, TV shows, columnists, journalists, newspapers, magazines, novelists, novels, bloggers, tweeters, or any other dataset). Restrict the network to a specific genre, geographic location, or predetermined size if desired. Discuss the science, understanding, and utility of modeling influence and impact within networks, including how the measures could be used to choose co-authors, graduate schools, or thesis advisors.
tasks.task_analysis: The algorithm is applied to a songwriter collaboration network, a domain completely different from mathematics. The network is a deterministic model of 50 influential songwriters (1980s-2010s) plus 10 one-off collaboration artists (Case C tail), structured to reflect the real-world collaboration patterns of the songwriting field: a dense core of hit-making collaborators within four sub-genres (pop/rock, country/folk, hip-hop/R&B, independent/alternative), cross-genre bridges (degree-2 nodes linking two sub-genres, Case B), and a long tail of one-off collabs (Case C). The same two-term influence measure from Task 2 is applied, demonstrating that the algorithm generalizes to a different domain: the same structural measures (degree + endpoint-importance-weighted betweenness) identify the most influential songwriters regardless of the specific collaboration data. The utility discussion addresses how the influence measures could be used to make practical decisions: choosing co-authors (target high-influence researchers who are well-connected but not saturated), selecting graduate schools (target programs with high aggregate influence and strong bridging researchers), and choosing thesis advisors (target advisors with high influence and high endpoint-importance, i.e., those embedded in the influential core).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
The songwriter network is a deterministic graph G = (V, E) with |V| = 60 (50 named songwriters + 10 tail artists) and edges defined by collaboration. The generator constructs: (1) within-genre collaboration at probability 0.35 for four sub-genres (pop/rock 20 nodes, country/folk 10 nodes, hip-hop/R&B 10 nodes, independent/alternative 10 nodes), producing dense cores (Case A); (2) three cross-genre bridges: degree-2 nodes linking pop<->country, pop<->hip-hop, and pop<->indie (Case B, the thin-bridge failure mode); and (3) 10 tail nodes that are isolated or in tiny components (Case C). The same two-term influence measure is applied:

    influence(v) = 0.5 * minmax(max(deg(v), deg_floor=2.0))
                 + 0.5 * minmax(BC(v) * (0.5 + 0.5 * EI(v)))

where EI(v) = minmax(mean degree of v's neighbors) is the endpoint-importance weight. The uncorrected blend is also computed for comparison. The Case-B bridge is detected as a degree-2 articulation point whose removal leaves two components of size >= 5.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The songwriter network has n = 60, m = 125, mean degree 4.167, max degree 12, 6 connected components, LCC size 54 (LCC fraction 0.9). The top-5 influence ranking is: (1) Babyface (score 1.0, degree 12, BC 589.5), (2) Arrif Mabb (score 0.8261, degree 10, BC 504.5), (3) Steve Johnstone (score 0.5418, degree 4, BC 464.6), (4) Elliott Smith (score 0.5236, degree 6, BC 434.0), (5) Kris Kristofferson (score 0.4675, degree 6, BC 410.0). The top-2 researchers (Babyface, Arrif Mabb) have both high degree and high betweenness, confirming that the measure correctly identifies the hit-making collaborators at the center of the pop/rock core (Case A). The Case-B bridge (Artist 1, vertex 50, degree 2, BC 430.0) is ranked 11th in the uncorrected measure (inflated by its raw betweenness, which is 430.0 — nearly as high as the top-5 researchers' betweenness) and 9th in the corrected measure. The correction (degree floor + endpoint-importance weighting) moves the bridge up 2 ranks because the bridge's neighbors are high-degree (the pop and country hubs), giving it a high EI weight, but the degree floor still suppresses its overall score. This demonstrates that the Case-B correction works in a different domain: the thin bridge is not ranked at the top (where a raw betweenness measure would place it), but it is also not collapsed to zero (because it does connect two influential clusters). The utility of influence modeling is threefold: (1) for individuals, the measure identifies high-influence, well-connected researchers who are good co-author targets (target the top decile of the influence ranking, but avoid saturated hubs by checking degree); (2) for graduate school selection, aggregate the influence scores of a program's faculty to rank programs, and identify bridging researchers (high betweenness, high EI) who can connect a student to multiple sub-fields; (3) for thesis advisor selection, target advisors with high influence and high endpoint-importance (embedded in the influential core), and check their bridging role (betweenness) to ensure they can expose the student to multiple research communities. The model's strength is that it separates prolificity (degree) from bridging (betweenness) and corrects for the thin-bridge failure mode; its weakness is that it relies on the collaboration network alone and does not capture the quality of the work (a prolific but unimportant researcher scores high), which is why the paper-influence model (Task 3) uses a role weight to capture the importance of the work itself.
